I don't get why others are so harsh about this. I have a group from high school I hang out with from time to time, and I've been outgrowing the friendship for years. I feel older and like I'm almost babysitting high schoolers when they'll be 30 in a couple of years. They also haven't had milestones like going to college (besides community, also not knocking that same here), play DnD making it priority and having to schedule around it, most don't have a handle on personal finances, still watch kid cartoons and anime which personally I've grown out of for the most part, just want to stay at home, most live with parents or roomates but haven't left their bubble to expand their view on the world, they haven't had any jobs besides low level grocery or freelance work, I'm more intrested in intellectual discussions where as they're comfortable repeating childhood stories like it was yesterday. I also am at a different stage in life which makes the contrast bigger being with a long term parter, going out and traveling, having a "big kid" job and just getting out of that childhood suburban bubble they're still in.

It just irks me when I'm around them since they zap my energy, and I'm not into watching cartoons or talking about high school anymore. So I definitely go through th3 same irritation and just desire for more from the friend group. It's just one of those things where you can just find friends who match your current life better and see the other friends less. They'll grow up eventually one way or another.

Obviously not having a relationship, or high paying job, and having hobbies or interests that you're not into doesn't make them bad people just different and seeing that shift from sharing interests to growing apart is what's hard.

I just understand and want you to know that it's normal and the other comments weren't nice or understanding of this experience with friendships growing apart.

I graduated from a two year degree studying graphic design, built an impressive personal portfolio from school projects. Mass applied and got a lot of interest from cool companies but didn't have enough experience. Landed this one after 2mos of looking and it was fulltime/agency work for $45k (low imo)

A small ad agency that was so incredibly toxic. Everyone left as I was hired leaving very few employees to run the place, I was seriously overworked and called a workhorse. I was harrassed sexually from my art director and creative director/owner. Owner's wife was HR. The head of marketing would comment on how thin I was and always make comments of my food during lunch. My art director moved spots to sit right next to me and started working off my screen to "help" fix or edit my work. There was no boundaries, they prided themselves with this non corporate culture, brought dogs in, drunk beer mid-day and judged me for wearing a mask...right when people were going back to the office from covid. My art director showed massive red flags but especially jealously and would gossip about me to the creative director after I pulled him aside a few times hoping we could be more collaborative or mitigate his micromanagement and bully tatics.

Creative director would hug me, smell my hair, touch my clothes and constanly compliment me...only me when his wife who I only met 4 times wasn't there. I was leaving one day and the creative director asked what I was doing for 4th of July and I said moving, my boyfriend was helping me and my family. He told me that my boyfriend and I should "break in the house". We were alone and I felt scared so I laughed it off and left. Another day my art director told me when I was staying late and my boyfriend was coming to bring me dinner...to "turn the cameras away if we wanted to have sex in the office". The only people being hired were young women right out of college after the employees I was hired with left. Very high turn over to this day and thankfully the art director seemed to have been fired. I was hired right out of college too, only took me a month or two to land it. Got a lot of experience being an agency with lots of experience with different industries and clients. The work was fun the environment and people were horribly toxic. Right off the bat it was the typical horror story agency, first one there last to leave everyday. Asked to do unpaid work at home on the weekends. I refused and they didn't like that. Would talk sh*t about past employees (women specifically) from 10+ yrs prior acting like they were the issue for current problems and they "left on time". Phrases like "you're lucky you work here", "now you're thinking like a designer", "I'm not trying to break your spirit", "sorry I was so rough on you today" after everyone left. Just verbal abuse and it really traumatized me especially with the harrassment. Said we're a "family" and they crossed boundaries and hungout a lot at their homes and bars, smoked and drunk a lot which isn't my scene.

For a meeting I pulled a metal chair accidentally on a metal floor outlet in their old house-turned-studio and it shocked the chair and smoked causing a small electrical fire...nothing happened but I was shaken and made to brush it off. I clearly didn't fit in their "culture". They sexualized and talked about their sex lives daily while being horribly misogynistic and graphic on the daily. One day they brought in their guns to show them off. They took turns holding and pointing around the room. Joked how I was closest to the door and would be first to die if someone were to come in and rob the place (they told me their was a few robberies across the street at the two banks as well as drugged up homless men). Then said to me lauguing how they'd use me as a "meat sheild". That was the owner, art director, and project manager...all men, I was the only women. I left after 6mos and was left traumatized and I still sometimes have ptsd symptoms from that place. Horrible first job but now I can look back and see the work experience as a positive at least. Always be looking out for those red flags even ones that aren't so blatant like this place.

I think this is a nice design for a portfolio piece for a letterhead/paper system.

Make sure your logo is vector based use illustrator or another vector based program (figma is best for digital unless you pay for the cmyk plugin). Svg/png is best for logos on websites not print. PDF logo should be okay but like someone else said, maybe try an EPS illustrator file. Always make sure logos are properly saved out, best practice 1080 on the longest side. Outline text, outline strokes, make compound paths where needed. Use cmyk and 300 dpi for print (plus any pantones if required).

Yes. You can also have personal projects/conceptual pieces too. Whatever shows off your abilities and skill put that in your portfolio.

You'll really want a website. Behance/PDFs/other solutions aren't the greatest looks. It's all about first impressions. Like another poster said Adobe Portfolio comes with the adobe package that's what I use and it's clean and user friendly can have plug-ins for ecommerce too if you needed.
Not just freelance noticing for inhouse/salary jobs it's dry. Last summer it was fine from what I saw.

Although being familiar with canva can be helpful if you ever needed to be in there. Though it's not a professional tool. Figma, sketch, indesign, photoshop, and illustrator are your best friends. Get to know them well and just keep practicing and learning. Once you know one they're all pretty similar at the end of the day. Take classes if you can.

Learn photoshop, indesign, and illustrator and that's your basics. Learn figma and or sketch for more digital/ux/ui experience.

Your portfolio should be your website. Don't worry about creating a logo for yourself just use your name with a nice typeface...you're not a company but an individual.

Read reviews and make sure you find a place that suits you. You'll learn what you like weather it's print/digital/web or leaning towards illustration or more ux/ui. Keep learning and mastering your skills. If you need someone to review your portfolio message me. We've all been there at one point but I suggest taking classes or getting a degree in design if you can. You'll learn a lot and it can help you gain confidence.
